claims.text: Partial recrystallization of cold-rolled Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr can produce a heterogeneous, bimodal grain structure.
The heterogeneous grain structure can simultaneously produce yield strength above 1200 MPa and uniform elongation above 15% at room temperature.
A grain-size gradient generates back-stress strengthening and gradient-induced plasticity.
Coarse grains improve ductility by accommodating strain, whereas fine grains and grain boundaries increase yield strength through Hall-Petch and back-stress effects.
Lattice distortion arising from the random distribution of multiple principal elements provides solid-solution strengthening.
Maintaining a continuous BCC matrix prevents brittle fracture.
Avoiding a continuous ordered B2 phase prevents the brittleness associated with such a phase.
A heterogeneous structure avoids the low strength attributed to a single-phase weakly ordered BCC condition.
Room-temperature deformation of Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will be dominated by screw-dislocation motion.
Deformation twinning may occur if stacking-fault energy is sufficiently low, and Mo addition facilitates this twinning.
The as-cast equimolar Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a coarse-grained, single-phase BCC structure.
Cold rolling by 50–70% followed by annealing at 1000–1100 °C for 1–2 hours will create a nano-to-microscale grain-size gradient without full recrystallization.
The treated alloy will exhibit a yield strength of 1250 ± 100 MPa, uniform elongation of 18 ± 3%, and total elongation of 25 ± 4%.
Optimizing the Mo/Ti ratio can preserve BCC phase stability while reducing heavy-element content.
The optimized alloy will have a density of approximately 9.5–10.0 g/cm³, with a predicted value near 9.8 g/cm³.
The as-cast equimolar Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr baseline typically has yield strength above 1000 MPa and ductility below 5% because of brittle BCC behavior and inadequate strain hardening.
The approach requires Mo content and annealing conditions that do not produce a brittle intermetallic phase such as a Laves phase.
The grain-size gradient must survive annealing because full recrystallization would eliminate the proposed back-stress effect.
Processing temperature must remain below the onset of phase decomposition or ordering that would embrittle the matrix.
Failure of the heterogeneous-grain batch to improve both yield strength and uniform elongation over both as-cast and homogeneous fine-grained controls would falsify the proposed HGS-driven synergy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says yield strength will exceed 1200 MPa, but the predicted range of 1250 ± 100 MPa includes values as low as 1150 MPa.

The tested material is specified as strictly equimolar, while density, phase stability, and property optimization are attributed to varying the Mo/Ti ratio; no modified composition is defined for that optimization.
